value.overview: The Black-thighed Grosbeak (Pheucticus tibialis) is a distinctive highland songbird of Central America. It is endemic to the mountains of Costa Rica and western Panama, where it inhabits humid forests, forest edges, second-growth vegetation, and shaded agricultural areas. The species is named for its dark thighs, which contrast with its otherwise warm brown, black, and white plumage. It is most often found in cool, elevated landscapes, especially along forested mountain slopes and ridges.
value.classification: The Black-thighed Grosbeak belongs to the cardinal family, Cardinalidae, and the genus Pheucticus. It is closely related to other grosbeaks of the Americas.
value.identification: Adults have a large, heavy bill and a boldly patterned body. The head and upperparts are mainly black, while the underparts are white with warm brown or chestnut coloring on the flanks and lower belly. A prominent white wing patch and white markings in the tail are visible in flight. The black thighs are a useful identification feature. Females and immature birds are generally duller and browner than adult males, with less sharply contrasting markings.
value.rangeHabitat: The Black-thighed Grosbeak has a restricted range in the highlands of Costa Rica and western Panama. In Costa Rica, it occurs mainly in the Cordillera de Talamanca and other suitable middle- and upper-elevation mountain forests, including areas around forest edges, clearings, second growth, and shaded farms. It is associated with humid montane forest and usually occupies elevations from roughly 1,000 to 2,500 meters, although local records may extend beyond this range. Protection of remaining highland forest is important for its habitat.
value.migrationStatus: It is generally considered resident in Costa Rica and across its small range, although individuals may make local or seasonal movements in response to food availability, weather, or breeding conditions. It is not known for long-distance migration.
value.breeding: The breeding season varies with locality and may correspond mainly to the wetter months. The species builds a fairly bulky, cup-shaped nest in vegetation, usually above the ground, and the female lays a small clutch of eggs. Both adults are believed to participate in caring for the young. Breeding commonly occurs in forest, forest margins, and dense secondary vegetation. Detailed information on nest placement, incubation, and parental roles is more limited than for many widespread grosbeak species.
value.dietFeeding: The Black-thighed Grosbeak feeds mainly on fruits, berries, seeds, and other plant material, and it may also take insects and other small invertebrates, particularly when feeding young. Its strong bill is suited to handling seeds and fleshy fruit. It usually forages in shrubs, small trees, and forest edges, sometimes moving through mixed-species flocks or visiting fruiting plants in disturbed but well-vegetated habitats.
value.behavior: This grosbeak is usually encountered singly, in pairs, or in small groups. It moves deliberately through dense vegetation while searching for fruit, seeds, and invertebrates. Males have a clear, musical song and may sing from exposed perches during the breeding season. The species can tolerate some habitat modification when cover and food-producing vegetation remain available, but it is closely tied to cool, forested mountain environments and is less commonly seen in heavily cleared areas.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population trend is not clearly established, and reliable estimates are limited. Habitat loss and fragmentation may cause local declines even though the species is not currently classified as globally threatened.
conservation.threats: Conversion and fragmentation of montane forest, agricultural expansion, road development, and degradation of forest edges may reduce suitable habitat. Climate change could also affect the availability and distribution of cool, humid highland environments.
conservation.howToHelp: Protect and restore high-elevation forest in Costa Rica, maintain wooded connections between mountain reserves, and support shade-grown farming practices that retain native trees and dense vegetation. Recording sightings through reputable bird-monitoring programs can improve knowledge of its distribution and population changes.
